paragraphs: A knapsack problem asks which items to select while staying within a budget. In the classical version, each item has a fixed value. This paper studies a different setting: an external function, such as a neural network, determines item values during optimization. The objective is to select a subset that maximizes the sum of those predicted values.

This changes the role of the neural network. Rather than using a network to predict a solution to a conventional knapsack problem, the researchers make the network part of the objective being optimized. The resulting nonlinear objective must still respect the budget constraint. They formulate a two-player game, drawing inspiration from game-theoretic methods in deep learning, and develop an adaptive gradient ascent method to solve it.

The experiments report successful solutions for two nonlinear knapsack problems with neural network objectives and for conventional linear problems containing one million items. These findings demonstrate the method on both the proposed setting and a large classical setting; they do not establish universal optimality for arbitrary neural objectives.
icml-2021-a-novel-method-to-solve-neural.tldr: A two-player game and adaptive gradient ascent tackle budget-constrained item selection when neural networks determine item values.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent depends strongly on its step sizes: the amounts by which training updates change the model. This paper revisits exponential and cosine schedules, two simple ways of changing those amounts over training that already have practical support. Its central contribution is to explain theoretically when these schedules work well.

The authors prove convergence rates for smooth nonconvex objectives, both with and without the additional Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. For objectives satisfying that condition, they also show that the schedules adapt to the noise in stochastic gradients. They achieve almost optimal performance without knowing the noise level or tuning their hyperparameters to it. This is a specific noise-adaptation result, rather than a claim that all tuning becomes unnecessary.

An empirical comparison on real datasets and deep learning architectures finds that the two schedules match or outperform several carefully tuned alternatives. Each requires at most two hyperparameters to tune. Together, the theory and experiments support these schedules as simple options whose performance can rival more elaborate strategies in the studied settings.
icml-2021-a-second-look-at-exponential-a.tldr: Exponential and cosine step-size schedules receive convergence guarantees and, under the PL condition, adapt to gradient noise without noise-specific tuning.

paragraphs: A prediction system may initially lack useful information yet still be able to request it. Active feature acquisition studies which unobserved features to obtain during evaluation. The challenge is sequential: each new observation can change both the prediction and which information would be most useful to collect next.

The paper reformulates the underlying decision process through generative modeling. It learns a generative surrogate model that captures relationships among input features and estimates the potential information gained by acquiring them. That model supplies intermediate rewards and auxiliary information to a decision-making policy. These signals help guide acquisition when there are many possible actions and useful rewards are otherwise sparse.

The authors also introduce active instance recognition, an unsupervised setting in which the unknown features themselves are the targets. Here, the goal is to learn about an individual instance cost-efficiently, without a separate prediction label. Experiments report considerably better performance than previous leading methods on both supervised and unsupervised tasks, supporting the use of learned feature dependencies to guide information gathering.
icml-2021-active-feature-acquisition-wit.tldr: A generative model of feature dependencies helps an acquisition policy choose which missing information to request next.

paragraphs: This paper treats clustering as locating k centers to serve n agents in a metric space. It asks whether a sufficiently large group could collectively benefit by abandoning the chosen centers and establishing a new one. This perspective makes fairness depend on coordinated group interests rather than only on the overall clustering cost.

The proposed notion, core fairness, rules out any coalition of at least n/k agents that could strictly reduce its total distance by moving together to a new center. The motivation assumes agents can coordinate and utilities are transferable. Because the criterion concerns total distance, it evaluates the group's combined benefit rather than requiring every member to improve individually.

The authors investigate existence, computational hardness, and approximation. They relax fairness in two ways: changing how much improvement a deviating group must achieve, and changing how large that group must be. They study these relaxations separately and together on lines, trees, and general metric spaces, designing corresponding approximation algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real data examine how the algorithms perform.
icml-2021-approximate-group-fairness-for.tldr: The paper defines clustering fairness through coordinated group deviations and develops algorithms for relaxed versions of that requirement.

paragraphs: Prediction risk describes how well a fitted model is expected to predict, but that risk can itself vary with the training sample. This paper studies such uncertainty for the minimum-norm least squares estimator in high-dimensional linear regression. Its focus is the variability of prediction performance, rather than only a single value summarizing that performance.

The authors establish asymptotic normality as both the number of observations and the number of features grow. Their central limit theorems describe the limiting fluctuations of prediction risk and provide the basis for confidence intervals under several scenarios. These intervals make uncertainty in the risk estimate explicit within the high-dimensional regimes analyzed.

The results show sample-wise nonmonotonicity: adding data can sometimes worsen prediction risk, confirming a possible “more data hurt” effect. They also find that confidence interval widths indicate greater randomness in prediction performance with overparameterization. The findings therefore concern both changes in risk and its variability; they do not say that additional data always harms prediction or that every overparameterized fit performs poorly.
icml-2021-asymptotic-normality-and-confi.tldr: New central limit theorems quantify uncertainty in minimum-norm regression risk and show that more data can sometimes worsen prediction performance.

paragraphs: Computing a truncated singular value decomposition across multiple machines requires combining information held on different nodes. Communication can become a significant part of that process. This paper introduces LocalPower, which partitions the dataset uniformly across m nodes and lets each node perform p local power iterations before a global aggregation.

The aggregation must combine local eigenvector matrices coherently. The authors propose using an orthogonal Procrustes transformation to align them. They also consider a simpler surrogate, sign-fixing, which applies positive or negative signs through a diagonal matrix. In experiments, sign-fixing offers better computational complexity and stability, making it a practical alternative to the fuller transformation.

Under stated assumptions, the analysis shows that LocalPower reduces the number of communications needed for constant accuracy by a factor of p. That guarantee is tied to the accuracy target and assumptions. For higher precision, the authors show that periodically reducing p helps: local work becomes more frequently coordinated as the solution is refined. Experiments further demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness.
icml-2021-communication-efficient-distri.tldr: LocalPower reduces communication in distributed SVD by alternating multiple local iterations with aligned global aggregations.

paragraphs: The paper studies decisions under uncertainty when the relevant probability distribution is unknown. The available evidence consists of finitely many correlated observations generated by an unknown Markov chain with d states. The authors propose a data-driven distributionally robust model to estimate both the optimization objective and its optimal solution.

Using large deviations theory, they derive statistical guarantees for these estimates. Computation presents a separate obstacle: the model's worst-case expectation problem is nonconvex and has on the order of d squared decision variables. This makes directly solving it inefficient when the chain has many states.

The proposed solution exploits a dual reformulation to reduce dimensionality. A customized Frank–Wolfe algorithm then uses convex direction-finding subproblems of size proportional to d. Under mild conditions, the authors prove that it efficiently reaches a stationary point, which is a weaker conclusion than finding a global optimum of the nonconvex problem. Numerical experiments indicate better computational and statistical properties than leading alternatives, supporting both the modeling approach and the specialized solver.
icml-2021-distributionally-robust-optimi.tldr: A robust optimization model handles correlated Markov-chain observations, with statistical guarantees and a specialized solver that efficiently finds stationary points.

paragraphs: Federated learning must serve devices whose data can differ substantially. This paper studies two goals in that setting: robustness against poisoned data or models, and fairness defined as uniform performance across devices. The authors identify that these goals can compete in networks with statistically heterogeneous data.

Their response is Ditto, a general framework for personalized federated learning, together with a scalable solver. Personalization allows the learning system to accommodate differences among devices. The paper investigates whether that flexibility can support both fairness and robustness, rather than treating either objective as an isolated design concern. Its theoretical analysis establishes results for a class of linear problems.

Across a suite of federated datasets, Ditto achieves performance competitive with recent personalization methods. Compared with leading baselines designed for fairness or robustness, it produces models that are more accurate, robust, and fair in the reported experiments. These results support personalization as a way to address the competing objectives, while the theoretical claim remains scoped to the analyzed linear problems and fairness retains its device-performance definition.
icml-2021-ditto-fair-and-robust-federate.tldr: Ditto uses personalized federated learning to improve device-level fairness and robustness to poisoning, with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: Steerable convolutional networks build knowledge about geometric transformations into their architecture. The intended behavior may be invariance, where a transformation leaves the response unchanged, or equivariance, where the response changes correspondingly. Such structure is used to improve robustness to transformed inputs and reduce overfitting.

A longstanding construction augments a filter with transformed copies of itself. The paper calls this filter transform. A separate theoretical perspective uses group representation theory to describe the space of valid steerable kernels. The authors address the missing connection between this practical construction and the more formal description of what steerable kernels can look like.

They show that kernels produced by filter transform can also be understood through group representation theory. This links an intuitive construction to the theoretical framework and yields a simple way to implement steerable convolution operators. Experiments on multiple datasets verify the feasibility of the approach. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and practical: it clarifies why the construction fits the theory and turns that connection into an implementation method.
icml-2021-filtra-rethinking-steerable-cn.tldr: FILTRA connects transformed copies of convolutional filters to group representation theory and uses that connection to implement steerable convolutions.

paragraphs: Machine translation can admit multiple valid outputs for the same input. This paper proposes mixed cross entropy as a replacement for standard cross entropy in two ways of training autoregressive translation models: teacher forcing and scheduled sampling. The motivation is to change how training represents acceptable outputs and relates to prediction at test time.

Under teacher forcing, the authors describe standard cross entropy as treating translation as a one-to-one mapping. Mixed cross entropy relaxes that treatment toward a one-to-many relationship. Under scheduled sampling, they argue that the replacement has the potential to make training and testing behavior more similar, thereby mitigating exposure bias more effectively.

Experiments on Romanian–English, Russian–English, and English–German translation datasets show improvements over standard cross entropy under both training approaches. On the English–German task, mixed cross entropy also consistently performs better with multiple references and challenging paraphrased references. The authors additionally report a better probability distribution over possible translation outputs. These findings support the loss as a way to accommodate output diversity while improving the evaluated translation models.
icml-2021-mixed-cross-entropy-loss-for-n.tldr: Mixed cross entropy improves the evaluated translation models while allowing training to better accommodate multiple valid translations.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often struggles to discover how to reach a goal. Human demonstrations can help, but collecting complete demonstrations may be costly. MURAL instead studies tasks specified by examples of successful outcome states. These examples describe what success looks like without requiring a supervisor to demonstrate the entire route to it.

A classifier can turn those examples into a learned reward by predicting whether a state is successful. The paper argues that useful guidance requires predictions that account for uncertainty, which standard deep-network training handles poorly in this setting. Its solution approximates a normalized maximum likelihood distribution using an amortized computation made tractable through meta-learning.

The resulting uncertainty-aware rewards connect to count-based exploration and earlier reward-learning algorithms, while providing more effective guidance toward goals. Experiments show that MURAL solves challenging navigation and robotic manipulation tasks that are difficult or impossible for prior methods in the evaluation. The contribution joins a less demanding form of task supervision with a specific uncertainty mechanism that helps make the learned rewards useful for exploration.
icml-2021-mural-meta-learning-uncertaint.tldr: MURAL uses meta-learning to build uncertainty-aware rewards from successful outcome examples, improving exploration on evaluated navigation and manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Online load balancing assigns work as it arrives. This paper studies how learned predictions can help in the unrelated-machine setting, where assigning a job to different machines can incur different processing costs. It develops both the machinery for turning fractional assignments into actual assignments and a prediction scheme that supplies those fractional assignments.

For m machines, the deterministic rounding algorithm achieves an O(log m / log log m) competitive ratio. The randomized algorithm achieves O(log log m / log log log m). Both improve the corresponding previous bounds and match the cited lower bounds. These guarantees quantify assignment quality relative to an optimum, rather than reporting empirical speed improvements.

The authors also extend a prediction scheme previously used in a more restricted machine setting. Given two machine-indexed vectors, a dual vector and a weight vector, their method constructs a good fractional assignment online and passes it to a rounding algorithm. Under the learning model they study, both vectors can be learned efficiently from a few sampled instances, connecting the improved rounding guarantees to learnable predictions.
icml-2021-online-unrelated-machine-load-.tldr: Improved online rounding algorithms and two learnable prediction vectors extend prediction-assisted load balancing to unrelated machines.

paragraphs: Microelectrode-dot-array biochips move extremely small droplets to execute biochemical protocols. Moving several droplets in parallel supports higher throughput, but microelectrodes degrade over time, complicating reliable control. Earlier reinforcement-learning work could account for electrode health, yet the approach described here could not transport multiple droplets concurrently and required cameras to monitor movement.

The paper introduces a multi-agent reinforcement-learning solution for droplet routing. It supports parallel transportation on different sizes of biochips equipped with integrated sensors. This directly addresses both stated limitations: coordinating multiple droplets and using a sensing arrangement that does not depend on the earlier camera-based setup.

The authors demonstrate reliable execution of a serial-dilution bioassay on a fabricated chip using their learned router. This physical demonstration supports the method's relevance to actual fluidic operations, beyond a routing formulation alone. They also provide a simulation environment using the PettingZoo Gym Interface to support further multi-agent routing research. The reported result concerns bioassay execution and droplet control, rather than a measured improvement in clinical diagnostic accuracy.
icml-2021-parallel-droplet-control-in-me.tldr: A multi-agent reinforcement-learning router coordinates droplets on sensor-equipped biochips and demonstrates reliable serial dilution on fabricated hardware.

paragraphs: When some features of an instance are missing, its observed features can help predict the rest. Related instances may offer additional information, but many approaches model dependencies only within one instance at a time. This paper introduces partially observed exchangeable modeling, or POEx, to use both sources of information together.

POEx receives a set of related, partially observed instances and infers conditional distributions for unobserved dimensions across multiple set elements. It jointly models relationships among features within a point and relationships among points in the set. The central change is therefore the scope of conditioning: observed information from the related collection can inform what remains unknown.

The framework covers existing applications such as point cloud expansion and few-shot generation, while also introducing tasks such as few-shot imputation. These applications share the need to infer missing or new information using limited related observations. Extensive empirical evaluations report state-of-the-art performance across a range of applications. The results suggest that modeling within-instance and between-instance dependencies jointly can be useful across several tasks rather than only one specialized completion problem.
icml-2021-partially-observed-exchangeabl.tldr: POEx predicts unobserved features by jointly modeling dependencies within individual instances and across related partially observed instances.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving machine learning often concentrates on training and prediction, even though preprocessing also handles sensitive data. This paper addresses feature selection: deciding which input variables to keep. It proposes a secure multiparty computation protocol for filter-based selection, so features can be assessed independently of a particular model's training procedure.

The method uses an efficient secure scoring protocol based on Gini impurity. Its separation from training allows it to work with other MPC protocols for feature ranking. The authors evaluate an outsourced service configuration in which multiple servers perform the computation, considering both semi-honest and malicious adversaries. This places the preprocessing step within explicit security settings rather than assuming trusted computation.

On a variety of real-world datasets, the proposed secure selection improves classifier accuracy while revealing neither feature values nor the identities of selected features. Reported runtimes range from seconds to an hour, depending on dataset size and security settings. The findings show practical feasibility across the tested configurations, while also making clear that the computational cost varies substantially with the workload and protection requirements.
icml-2021-privacy-preserving-feature-sel.tldr: Secure multiparty computation enables feature selection that hides both feature values and selected features while improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning with incorrect labels often relies on a transition matrix describing how clean labels become noisy ones. Estimating this matrix can help produce statistically consistent classifiers. Existing consistent estimators use anchor points, but the assumption that such points exist does not always hold in real data.

This paper proposes an end-to-end framework that learns without anchor points. It simultaneously optimizes cross entropy between observed noisy labels and network predictions, and the volume of a simplex formed by the transition matrix's columns. The geometric objective adds structure to matrix estimation alongside the objective that fits the observed labels.

The guarantee depends on clean class-posterior probabilities being sufficiently scattered. Under that condition, the framework can identify the transition matrix and learn a statistically consistent classifier. The authors characterize this as the mildest known assumption supporting those conclusions. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effectiveness and robustness. The advance therefore removes the anchor-point requirement while retaining an explicit alternative condition that makes recovery provable; it does not claim that arbitrary label corruption can be resolved without assumptions.
icml-2021-provably-end-to-end-label-nois.tldr: Joint prediction and geometric optimization recover label-noise transitions without anchor points when clean class probabilities are sufficiently scattered.

paragraphs: Random Fourier features approximate the nonlinear Gaussian kernel by transforming randomly projected data. Quantizing those features can make storage, computation, and transmission more efficient. This paper develops quantization methods specifically for random Fourier features, where the Gaussian kernel's tuning parameter might otherwise complicate the design of a reusable quantizer.

The key finding comes from analyzing the features' probability distributions. Their marginal distribution does not depend on the kernel parameter gamma. The authors use this property to simplify a Lloyd–Max quantization scheme: one quantizer can be used regardless of gamma. The independence concerns the marginal feature distribution and resulting quantizer design, rather than a claim that the Gaussian kernel itself is independent of its parameter.

The paper also analyzes the resulting kernel estimators and approximation error, connecting compression decisions to the quality of the kernel approximation. Experiments confirm the proposed method's effectiveness and efficiency. Together, these results provide a distribution-based route to compact random Fourier features and avoid the need to design a separate Lloyd–Max quantizer for each kernel parameter.
icml-2021-quantization-algorithms-for-ra.tldr: A parameter-independent marginal distribution enables one Lloyd–Max quantizer for random Fourier features across Gaussian kernel parameter choices.

paragraphs: Clustering generalization theory asks how well a clustering learned from a sample performs beyond that sample. This paper introduces a unified learning framework instead of analyzing only particular methods. It studies excess clustering risk, with bounds expressed in terms of sample size n and number of clusters K.

For the general framework, the authors obtain an O(K squared / n) upper bound under mild assumptions on the covering number of the hypothesis space. Covering numbers describe the space's complexity through how many approximating elements are needed. The authors describe these assumptions as easy to verify, in contrast to strong distributional assumptions used for earlier bounds of the same order.

For hard clustering, including ordinary and kernel k-means, bounded hypothesis functions alone yield an O(square root of K / square root of n) bound, improving the previous linear dependence on K. With the covering-number assumptions, they obtain the faster O(K / n) order. These are conditional upper bounds on excess risk: their importance is tighter control of sample and cluster-count dependence under the specified assumptions.
icml-2021-sharper-generalization-bounds-.tldr: A unified clustering framework yields sharper excess-risk bounds, including O(K/n) for hard clustering under covering-number assumptions.

paragraphs: Training very large language models requires distributing their computation across machines. TeraPipe identifies an additional way to organize that work: pipeline execution within a single training sequence. The autoregressive structure of Transformer language models makes this possible, exposing finer-grained units of work than earlier pipeline approaches.

The system uses token-level pipeline parallelism for synchronous model-parallel training. It also introduces a dynamic programming algorithm that calculates an optimal pipelining execution scheme for a specified model and cluster configuration. This makes execution planning part of the method, with the schedule tailored to the particular computation and hardware arrangement.

For the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 model on an AWS cluster containing 48 p3.16xlarge instances, the authors report a 5.0-fold training speedup over leading model-parallel methods. That result is tied to the stated configuration rather than a universal acceleration factor. The broader contribution is identifying within-sequence pipelining as a dimension orthogonal to existing model-parallel approaches, together with a scheduling method that makes that finer-grained parallelism useful in the demonstrated large-scale training setup.
icml-2021-terapipe-token-level-pipeline-.tldr: TeraPipe pipelines tokens within training sequences and reports a 5.0-fold speedup for a specified 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 training configuration.

paragraphs: Testing a neural-network-based driving system involves understanding when errors become more likely. This paper focuses on environmental conditions, rather than only collecting individual erroneous behaviors. It calls conditions critical when the driving system is more prone to errors under them, making the environment itself an object of systematic testing.

The proposed approach, TACTIC, combines search with an image-to-image translation model. The model generates images representing environmental conditions, while the search procedure seeks critical ones within an extremely large space of possibilities. This gives the testing process a way to direct attention toward conditions associated with failures instead of attempting exhaustive coverage.

Large-scale experiments show that TACTIC produces realistic testing images and effectively identifies critical environmental conditions. It also exposes more erroneous behaviors than the existing approaches used in the comparison. These findings support the combination of generated environmental variation and targeted search as a testing strategy. Its demonstrated contribution is improved discovery of problematic conditions and behaviors, providing evidence about where an evaluated driving system is vulnerable.
icml-2021-testing-dnn-based-autonomous-d.tldr: TACTIC searches image-generated environmental conditions to uncover situations where neural driving systems are more likely to make errors.

paragraphs: Bandits with knapsacks extend sequential action selection to include limited resources. An action must be judged by both its reward and its resource consumption. This paper seeks a problem-dependent regret guarantee, making the bound sensitive to the particular instance rather than relying only on distribution-free worst-case behavior.

The authors analyze the problem's primal and dual linear programs and identify a symmetry between actions, called arms, and resource budgets, called knapsacks. They introduce a suboptimality measure that reflects the role of both. This motivates a two-phase algorithm: first identify optimal arms and binding resource constraints, then adaptively use those arms to exhaust the binding budgets.

The resulting regret bound grows logarithmically with the time horizon and polynomially with the numbers of arms and knapsacks. It also depends on the proposed suboptimality measure, so the logarithmic result retains its instance-dependent qualification. The authors describe it as the first such guarantee for the general problem. The conceptual contribution is showing that learning which resources constrain the optimum matters alongside learning which actions are best.
icml-2021-the-symmetry-between-arms-and-.tldr: A primal-dual bandit algorithm identifies both optimal actions and binding budgets to achieve a problem-dependent logarithmic regret bound.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups data points that lie near a collection of subspaces. A common approach first constructs a random geometric graph and then applies spectral clustering to that graph. The graph can contain false connections, so understanding its construction alone does not fully explain the quality of the final clustering.

This paper focuses on the second step. The authors argue that earlier theoretical work largely studied graph construction while overlooking how spectral clustering can correct false connections. They analyze a simplified algorithm under a widely used semi-random model to explain the mechanism by which the spectral step contributes to successful clustering.

Using that analysis, they prove the efficiency of subspace clustering under fairly broad conditions within the studied setting. The result gives theoretical attention to a stage that is essential to the complete procedure, rather than evaluating success solely through the initial graph. The authors also suggest that their insights and analytical techniques might inform other random-graph problems. That broader relevance is presented as a possibility, while the established results concern the analyzed subspace-clustering model.
icml-2021-theory-of-spectral-method-for-.tldr: The paper explains theoretically how spectral clustering can correct false graph connections in subspace clustering under a semi-random model.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models can express stereotypes that propagate harmful generalizations about social groups. This paper focuses on these representational biases, including those involving gender, race, and religion. Its aim is to make the biases more clearly defined and measurable, then use that understanding to improve generated text.

The authors first distinguish several sources of representational bias. They then propose benchmarks and metrics for measuring them, providing an evaluation basis for mitigation. With those tools in place, they develop steps to reduce social bias during text generation. The approach treats preserving relevant contextual information as part of the objective, alongside reducing harmful representations.

Empirical results and human evaluation indicate that the proposed methods mitigate bias while retaining context needed for high-fidelity generation. The authors describe this as advancing the performance–fairness Pareto frontier: achieving better combinations of generation quality and fairness in their evaluation. The finding supports an improved tradeoff on the biases and tasks studied, rather than establishing that generated language is free of all social bias.
icml-2021-towards-understanding-and-miti.tldr: The paper defines and measures representational biases, then demonstrates mitigation that preserves contextual information in generated text.

paragraphs: Deep graph neural networks must handle large graphs as well as the intermediate activations produced during training. This creates a substantial memory obstacle. While earlier approaches reduce the graph processed at a time through sampling or partitioning, this paper investigates architectural techniques that improve memory and parameter efficiency.

The authors study reversible connections, group convolutions, weight tying, and equilibrium models. Their key empirical finding is that combining reversible connections with deep architectures makes it possible to train overparameterized graph networks that significantly outperform existing methods on multiple datasets. The contribution links architectural efficiency to the ability to explore much deeper and wider models.

Two reported models are RevGNN-Deep, with 1001 layers and 80 channels per layer, and RevGNN-Wide, with 448 layers and 224 channels. Both train on a single commodity GPU. On ogbn-proteins, their reported ROC-AUC values are 87.74 ± 0.13 and 88.14 ± 0.15, respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility and evaluated performance of the architectures; the authors also describe the deeper model as an order of magnitude deeper than prior GNNs.
icml-2021-training-graph-neural-networks.tldr: Reversible architectures enable a 1001-layer graph neural network to train on one commodity GPU and achieve strong evaluated performance.

paragraphs: Knowledge transferability concerns how effectively a pretrained model can be adapted to a downstream task. Adversarial transferability concerns whether examples designed to attack one model can also attack another. This paper studies the relationship between these two phenomena to better understand what makes learned knowledge transferable.

The authors' theoretical analysis shows that adversarial transferability indicates knowledge transferability, and that the relationship also works in the reverse direction. Guided by these results, they propose two practical adversarial-transferability metrics. The metrics are intended to characterize the connection and act as indicators between successful knowledge transfer and successful attack transfer.

Experiments across diverse datasets and scenarios find a positive correlation between the two forms of transferability. This empirical association supports the theoretical connection and suggests that examining transferred attacks can provide information relevant to transfer learning. The result is about linked behavior and useful indicators; a positive correlation does not mean that every transferable attack guarantees a successful downstream adaptation. The work offers a shared perspective for studying model reuse and adversarial behavior.
icml-2021-uncovering-the-connections-bet.tldr: Theoretical analysis and experiments connect the transferability of adversarial attacks with the transferability of pretrained knowledge.
